name: Missing Do Not Sell Link
description: We did not detect a “Do Not Sell My Personal Information” link on your homepage. The absence of this control means users do not have an easy way to opt out of the sale of their personal information, which may result in non-compliance with CCPA and similar privacy laws. If this finding is not part of your organization’s compliance obligations, you can resolve the finding using “Accepted Risk”.
recommendation: Adding a clear “Do Not Sell My Personal Information” link to your website's homepage that allows users to opt out of the sale of their personal data.,If this link already exists and our detection failed, mark this finding as incorrectly identified.,Mark this finding as “Accepted Risk” if your business determines that it is not required to implement this privacy control.
references: [Compliant "Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information" Page](https://termly.io/resources/articles/do-not-sell-my-personal-information/),[California CCPA: Do Not Sell Requirement](https://oag.ca.gov/privacy/ccpa#sectionb),[Managing downstream risks of 'do not sell' fulfillment](https://iapp.org/news/a/managing-downstream-risks-of-do-not-sell-fulfillment)

name: No Global Privacy Control
description: Our website analysis identified that your site does not recognize or process Global Privacy Control (GPC) signals. While your site uses tracking technologies like analytics or third-party cookies, it lacks the technical configuration to automatically honor opt-out requests sent via user browsers. Many US state-level privacy regulations require businesses to treat GPC signals as an opt-out request. For example, the California Attorney General has clarified that the GPC “must be honored by covered businesses as a valid consumer request to stop the sale or sharing of personal information”.
recommendation: Updating your website’s configuration or Consent Management Platform (CMP) to automatically detect and honor the GPC signal.,Ensuring that when a GPC signal is detected, the site automatically disables non-essential tracking and treats the signal as an objection to data sharing or sale.,Mark this finding as “Accepted Risk” if your business determines that it is not required to implement this privacy control.
references: [Global Privacy Control (GPC) Official Website: Technical specifications and implementation guides](https://globalprivacycontrol.org/),[State of California Department of Justice’s guidance on Global Privacy Control (GPC)](https://oag.ca.gov/privacy/ccpa/gpc),[Guide to Global Privacy Control and universal opt outs](https://usercentrics.com/knowledge-hub/what-is-global-privacy-control-2/#global-privacy-control-and-international-data-privacy-regulations-5)

name: Non-necessary cookies instantly fire
description: Our scan identified that marketing or analytics cookies are installed before the user can take an action. This means users have no chance of reading disclosures and opting out of tracking. Litigants often allege this kind of website activity violates wiretapping laws.
recommendation: Removing these cookies to eliminate the risk.,Ensuring cookies only fire after a user has opted-in to tracking via a consent banner.
references: [What Are CIPA Claims, and How Can Businesses Defend Against Them?](https://www.burr.com/newsroom/articles/what-are-cipa-claims-and-how-can-businesses-defend-against-them),[The Millisecond Problem: How Pre-Consent Tracking Is Driving CIPA Lawsuits in 2026](https://www.loeb.com/en/insights/publications/2026/04/the-millisecond-problem-how-pre-consent-tracking-is-driving-cipa-lawsuits-in-2026)

name: Website May Ignore Global Privacy Control
description: Our scan visited your website with and without the Global Privacy Control header turned on. We did not observe a difference in the setting of analytics/marketing cookies, or the cookie banner. Modern privacy laws at the state level often require this signal to be respected, and there is an open question about its applicability under the GDPR.
recommendation: Disabling trackers to eliminate the risk.,Ensuring trackers do not fire if the user has enabled the Global Privacy Control.
references: [There's no opting-out of universal opt-outs (IAPP)](https://iapp.org/news/a/there-s-no-opting-out-of-universal-opt-outs),[Opt-Out Rights Under Privacy Laws](https://www.termsfeed.com/blog/opt-out-rights-privacy-laws/),[OOPS! States Crack Down on Opt-Out Preference Signal Compliance](https://www.freshfields.com/en/our-thinking/blogs/a-fresh-take/oops-states-crack-down-on-opt-out-preference-signal-compliance-102ls1x)

name: No Cookie Banner Detected
description: We did not detect a visible cookie banner, despite detecting tracking technologies on your website. Depending on where your customer base is located geographically, global privacy laws may require you to ensure that your website obtains opt-in consent before placing non-essential cookies on a visitor's device. Adopting a clear notice may reduce residual risk and also demonstrates a commitment to user privacy, which may significantly improve visitor trust. Warning: We only detect third-party cookie banners, and cannot detect niche/self-implemented cookie banners. Mark this finding as incorrectly identified if you have a cookie banner we didn’t detect.
recommendation: Implementing a Consent Management Platform (CMP) that blocks all non-essential scripts until the user clicks "Accept.",Mark this finding as “Accepted Risk” if your business determines that it is not required to implement this privacy control.
references: [EU: New EDPB guidelines on the scope of the 'cookie rule'](https://privacymatters.dlapiper.com/2023/11/eu-new-edpb-guidelines-on-the-scope-of-the-cookie-rule/),[Coalition's State of Web Privacy Report](https://web.coalitioninc.com/download-state-of-web-privacy-report.html),[Privacy Best Practices for Small & Midsize Businesses](https://cdn.intelligencebank.com/us/share/NMXD/vnB87/AYZWv/original/Coalition_Privacy-Best-Practices-Checklist)

name: Privacy Policy Older than 12 Months
description: A "set-and-forget" approach to your Privacy Policy may be  a significant compliance risk because data laws are currently evolving at their fastest pace in a decade. Many regulators, including the FTC and the California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA), have issued clear guidance stating that policies must reflect current operational realities. The CCPA is the most explicit major law regarding timing. Under California law, businesses are required to review and update their privacy policy at least once every 12 months. While the GDPR does not explicitly say "update every 365 days", it mandates that information be accurate and up-to-date (Article 12).
recommendation: Conducting a "Freshness" Audit: Reviewing your policy to ensure it mentions modern rights (like the right to correct data) and recently adopted technologies (like AI or session replay). Make sure to also change the “last updated date” after making changes.,Aligning with 2025 Laws: Updating your language to meet the specific requirements of most recent applicable laws as determined by your company.
